Song of Solomon — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Henry reads this book as a divine allegory of the love between Christ and his church of true believers.

Its images arise from the relationship and affection between a bridegroom and his promised bride.

Scripture often uses marriage as a picture of an especially close, firm and secure relationship.

Henry points readers to Psalm 45; Isaiah 54:5–6; 62:5; Jeremiah 2:2; 3:1; Ezekiel; Hosea; Matthew 9:15; 25:1; Revelation 21:2, 9; and Ephesians 5:27.

He believes every kind of believer and every circumstance that believers experience can be recognized somewhere in this song when the book is carefully compared with other Scriptures, with the Holy Spirit's help in response to prayer.

However, he warns that expositors and translators have often misunderstood its figurative language.

We must particularly consider the important differences between the customs of Europe and the ancient Near East.

The limited understanding of eastern customs possessed by many earlier translators and interpreters prevented them, in some cases, from rendering the expressions correctly.

Changes in European languages during the previous two or three centuries also affected how particular phrases were understood.

Expressions from other ages must not be judged uncritically according to modern assumptions.

Nevertheless, Henry concludes that the book's main themes, rightly understood, are consistent with the sincere Christian's affections and spiritual experience.

The title of the song (verse 1)

This is the Song of Songs, superior to every other song in Henry's reading.

It is wholly concerned with the glory of Jesus Christ and the love between him and the people he has redeemed.

The believer confesses sin while longing for Christ (verses 2–6)

The church, or more particularly the individual believer, speaks here as the bride of the Messiah, the King.

The kisses of his mouth represent assurances of pardon.

Those assurances fill believers with peace and joy in faith and cause them to overflow with hope through the Holy Spirit's power.

Gracious souls find their greatest pleasure in loving Christ and being loved by him.

His love is better and more desirable than any good the world can offer.

The name of Christ is no longer like perfume shut up in its container.

It is like perfume poured out: the gospel openly reveals the fullness and freeness of his grace.

Those whom Christ redeems and sanctifies are pictured as the young women who love and follow him wherever he goes (Revelation 14:4).

They ask him to draw them, giving spiritual life and strength through the Holy Spirit.

The more clearly we see Christ's glory, the more we recognize our inability to follow him as we should—and the more strongly we want to follow.

Notice how quickly this prayer receives an answer.

Those waiting at Wisdom's entrance are led into truth and comfort.

In the King's chamber, sorrows disappear.

Everything we enjoy spiritually comes from Christ, to whom we owe all gratitude.

We should remember his love with thanksgiving longer and more deeply than anything else.

Only sincere love is acceptable to him (Ephesians 6:24).

The daughters of Jerusalem may represent people who profess faith but are not yet established in it.

The bride is dark like the tents of nomadic Arabs, yet lovely as the splendid curtains in Solomon's palace.

Likewise, a believer is sinful and defiled by nature, yet made beautiful through divine grace and renewed in God's image.

Even after renewal, some sinful corruption remains.

Yet the believer is lovely because accepted in Christ.

Someone despised by the world may be precious in God's sight.

The bride's darkened appearance reflects the difficult treatment she endured.

Those belonging to the church as her mother—but not to God as Father—had acted harshly toward her.

Their demands caused hardships and made her neglect the care of her own soul.

Here is a picture of a poor and suffering woman chosen to marry a prince.

Christ's love similarly finds people burdened with sin, exhausted by labor and heavy with sorrow.

What a great change occurs when his love becomes known to them!

The believer asks Christ for guidance and rest (verses 7 and 8)

How affectionate is the title given to Christ: “You whom my soul loves.”

Those who truly love him may approach with boldness and humble confidence.

Are God's people under the noon-day heat of outward suffering or inward spiritual conflict?

Christ has rest for them.

Believers want to share fully in the privileges of Christ's flock and fear straying away from him more than any other danger.

God is ready to answer their prayers.

Follow the good old way and the footsteps left by faithful believers.

Learn from their example and listen to the guidance of trustworthy ministers—the under-shepherds.

Bring those entrusted to your care; they too are welcome.

Christians should pray that God will direct their earthly work, circumstances and employment so that their Savior remains before them at all times.

Christ praises the church, and the church values him (verses 9–17)

The Bridegroom praises the bride.

In Christ's eyes his believers are excellent and valuable, fitted to serve as instruments of his glory.

The ornaments used in that culture picture the spiritual gifts and graces Christ grants every true believer (Song 1:10–11).

The graces are many and depend upon one another.

The One who began this good work will also finish it.

The grace believers receive from Christ's fullness produces faith, loving affections and gratitude.

Yet Christ himself, not merely his gifts, is their greatest treasure.

Henry explains the word translated “camphire” as meaning “atonement or propitiation”.

Christ is precious because he is the propitiation for our sins.

No rival may occupy his place in the soul.

Believers desire him to remain in their hearts through the whole night of earthly troubles.

Christ delights in the good that his grace has produced within their souls.

Those made holy should give thanks for the grace that made them beautiful when by nature they were corrupted.

The bride's modest, humble gaze suggests simplicity and godly sincerity.

Her eyes are illuminated and guided by the Holy Spirit, the blessed Dove.

In response, the church praises Christ:

He is the perfect original; I am only a faint and imperfect copy.

Someone may be physically attractive but unpleasant in character.

Christ is both beautiful and delightful.

In verse 16, the believer praises the appointed means of grace through which faithful people enjoy fellowship with Christ.

Whether worshiping in God's courts, resting privately, doing daily work, lying sick in bed or even confined in prison, a sense of God's presence can turn any place into paradise.

Daily communion with the Father, Son and Holy Spirit gives the soul a living hope of an inheritance that cannot perish, be defiled or fade away.

classic_reading:
[Song.1.1]
Song of Solomon
This book is a Divine allegory, which represents the love between Christ and his church of true believers, under figures taken from the relation and affection that subsist between a bridegroom and his espoused bride; an emblem often employed in Scripture, as describing the nearest, firmest, and most sure relation: see Ps. 45; [Isa.54.5] Is. 54:5, [Isa.54.6] 6; [Isa.62.5] 62:5; [Jer.2.2] Jr 2:2; [2Cor.3.1] 3:1; also in Ezekiel, Hosea, and by our Lord himself, Matt. 9:15; 25:1: see also Rev. 21:2,9; Eph. 5:27. There is no character in the church of Christ, and no situation in which the believer is placed, but what may be traced in this book, as humble inquirers will find, on comparing it with other Scriptures, by the assistance of God the Holy Spirit, in answer to their supplications. Much, however, of the language has been misunderstood by expositors and translators. The difference between the customs and manners of Europe, and those of the East, must especially be kept in view. The little acquaintance with eastern customs possessed by most of our early expositors and translators, has in many cases prevented a correct rendering. Also, the changes in our own language, during the last two or three centuries, affect the manner in which some expressions are viewed, and they must not be judged by modern notions. But the great outlines, rightly interpreted, fully accord with the affections and experience of the sincere Christian.
Chapter 1
The title. (Song 1:1) The church confesses her deformity. (Song 1:2-6) The church beseeches Christ to lead her to the resting-place of his people. (Song [1Cor.7.8] 1:7,8) Christ's commendation of the church, Her esteem for Him. (Song 1:9-17)
Verse 1 This is "the Song of songs," excellent above any others, for it is wholly taken up with describing the excellences of Christ, and the love between him and his redeemed people.
[Song.1.2-Song.1.6]
Verses 2-6 The church, or rather the believer, speaks here in the character of the spouse of the King, the Messiah. The kisses of his mouth mean those assurances of pardon with which believers are favoured, filling them with peace and joy in believing, and causing them to abound in hope by the power of the Holy Ghost. Gracious souls take most pleasure in loving Christ, and being loved of him. Christ's love is more valuable and desirable than the best this world can give. The name of Christ is not now like ointment sealed up, but like ointment poured forth; which denotes the freeness and fulness of the setting forth of his grace by the gospel. Those whom he has redeemed and sanctified, are here the virgins that love Jesus Christ, and follow him whithersoever he goes, Rev. 14:4. They entreat him to draw them by the quickening influences of his Spirit. The more clearly we discern Christ's glory, the more sensible shall we be that we are unable to follow him suitably, and at the same time be more desirous of doing it. Observe the speedy answer given to this prayer. Those who wait at Wisdom's gate, shall be led into truth and comfort. And being brought into this chamber, our griefs will vanish. We have no joy but in Christ, and for this we are indebted to him. We will remember to give thanks for thy love; it shall make more lasting impressions upon us than any thing in this world. Nor is any love acceptable to Christ but love in sincerity, Eph. 6:24. The daughters of Jerusalem may mean professors not yet established in the faith. The spouse was black as the tents of the wandering Arabs, but comely as the magnificent curtains in the palaces of Solomon. The believer is black, as being defiled and sinful by nature, but comely, as renewed by Divine grace to the holy image of God. He is still deformed with remains of sin, but comely as accepted in Christ. He is often base and contemptible in the esteem of men, but excellent in the sight of God. The blackness was owing to the hard usage that had been suffered. The children of the church, her mother, but not of God, her Father, were angry with her. They had made her suffer hardships, which caused her to neglect the care of her soul. Thus, under the emblem of a poor female, made the chosen partner of a prince, we are led to consider the circumstances in which the love of Christ is accustomed to find its objects. They were wretched slaves of sin, in toil, or in sorrow, weary and heavy laden, but how great the change when the love of Christ is manifested to their souls!
[Song.1.7-Song.1.8]
Verse 7 ,8 Observe the title given to Christ, O Thou whom my soul loveth. Those that do so, may come to him boldly, and may humbly plead with him. Is it with God's people a noon-time of outward troubles, inward conflicts? Christ has rest for them. Those whose souls love Jesus Christ, earnestly desire to share in the privileges of his flock. Turning aside from Christ is what gracious souls dread more than anything else. God is ready to answer prayer. Follow the track, ask for the good old way, observe the footsteps of the flock, look what has been the practice of godly people. Sit under the direction of good ministers; beside the tents of the under shepherds. Bring thy charge with thee, they shall all be welcome. It will be the earnest desire and prayer of the Christian, that God would so direct him in his worldly business, and so order his situation and employment, that he may have his Lord and Saviour always before him.
[Song.1.9-Song.1.17]
Verses 9-17 The Bridegroom gives high praises of his spouse. In the sight of Christ believers are the excellent of the earth, fitted to be instruments for promoting his glory. The spiritual gifts and graces which Christ bestows on every true believer, are described by the ornaments then in use, Song [1Cor.10.11] 1:10,11. The graces of the saints are many, but there is dependence upon each other. He who is the Author, will be the Finisher of the good work. The grace received from Christ's fulness, springs forth into lively exercises of faith, affection, and gratitude. Yet Christ, not his gifts, is most precious to them. The word translated "camphire," signifies "atonement or propitiation." Christ is dear to all believers, because he is the propitiation for their sins. No pretender must have his place in the soul. They resolved to lodge him in their hearts all the night; during the continuance of the troubles of life. Christ takes delight in the good work which his grace has wrought on the souls of believers. This should engage all who are made holy, to be very thankful for that grace which has made those fair, who by nature were deformed. The spouse (the believer) has a humble, modest eye, discovering simplicity and godly sincerity; eyes enlightened and guided by the Holy Spirit, that blessed Dove. The church expresses her value for Christ. Thou art the great Original, but I am but a faint and imperfect copy. Many are fair to look at, yet their temper renders them unpleasant: but Christ is fair, yet pleasant. The believer, Song 1:16, speaks with praise of those holy ordinances in which true believers have fellowship with Christ. Whether the believer is in the courts of the Lord, or in retirement; whether following his daily labours, or confined on the bed of sickness, or even in a dungeon, a sense of the Divine presence will turn the place into a paradise. Thus the soul, daily having fellowship with the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, enjoys a lively hope of an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance above.

Christ and his church love one another (verses 1–7)

Believers are lovely because they are clothed in Christ's righteousness and fragrant with the graces of his Spirit.

They flourish under the refreshing rays of the Sun of Righteousness.

The lily of the East may grow tall while possessing a fragile stem.

So the church is weak in itself but strong in Christ who supports it.

The wicked, who do not love Christ, are like thorns that injure and destroy.

Sinful corruption is itself like thorns in the flesh.

But the lily now surrounded by thorns will one day be transplanted into a paradise without any thorn or briar.

The world is a barren tree for the soul.

Christ is a fruit-bearing tree.

People dried out by conviction of sin, fear of the law or earthly troubles may find rest under his shade.

But merely passing by this shade is insufficient.

We must sit beneath it, receiving and enjoying his protection.

Believers have tasted the goodness of the Lord Jesus.

His fruit consists of the privileges of the new covenant, bought by his blood and given through his Spirit.

His promises are sweet, but so are his commands.

Forgiveness is sweet, as is peace of conscience.

When our taste for sinful pleasures has been lost, divine consolation becomes especially precious.

Christ leads souls to find comfort through his appointed ordinances, like a banqueting house where believers feast with him.

The banner over them is Christ's love, shown in his death and his word.

How much better to be overwhelmed by love for Christ than by love for the world!

Even when Christ seems absent, he remains a very present help.

His people are held in his hands with extraordinary tenderness.

The soul, recognizing Christ nearby, fears losing communion with him.

We can grieve the Spirit through sinful attitudes.

Let those who enjoy his consolation be careful not to sin away their comfort.

Christ calls the church out of winter (verses 8–13)

The church delights in the prospect of deeper fellowship with Christ.

He alone can speak directly to the heart.

The believer sees him approaching.

Henry says this image may refer to the Old Testament believers' expectation of Christ's coming in human flesh.

Christ comes gladly to fulfill his saving mission, and he comes quickly.

Even if he seems to leave his people, the absence is brief; he returns with enduring loving-kindness.

The saints of earlier times saw him through sacrifices and ceremonial ordinances.

We also see him imperfectly, as through a lattice.

Christ calls newly converted people to rise from idleness and discouragement and leave behind sin and worldly vanity in order to enjoy fellowship with him.

Winter may represent years of ignorance and unfruitfulness, or the storms of conviction concerning guilt and danger.

Even the earliest, unripe fruits of holy living are pleasing to the One whose grace produced them.

These tokens of divine kindness encourage the soul to follow Christ more wholeheartedly.

Rise and leave the world and the flesh for fellowship with Christ.

All this change comes from the Sun of Righteousness and his gracious influence.

Christ protects and guides his church (verses 14–17)

The church is Christ's dove, returning to him as to Noah.

Christ is the Rock where the dove finds refuge from birds of prey.

He invites her to come boldly before the throne of grace.

There she has a great High Priest to hear and present her requests.

Speak freely.

Do not fear contempt or rejection.

Prayer is sweet and acceptable to God.

Those whom he sanctifies possess their true beauty.

The little foxes picture the first beginnings of sinful thoughts and desires, frivolous distractions, wasted visits, small departures from the truth and the desire to conform to the world.

Believers must put such things away, mortifying passions that would destroy new spiritual growth.

Whatever prevents progress in what is good should be removed.

Christ feeds among the lilies: he is graciously present with his people.

Even when believers feel abandoned, they should remember his kindness and resist temptation.

The shadows of Jewish ceremonial worship disappeared as the gospel day dawned.

And after a night of spiritual absence, a new day of consolation will come.

Christ will cross the mountains of Bether, the mountains that divide, and ultimately cross every obstacle to bring his people home to himself.

[Song.2.1-Song.2.7]
Chapter 2
The mutual love of Christ and his church. (Song 2:1-7) The hope and calling of the church. (Song 2:8-13) Christ's care of the church, Her faith and hope. (Song 2:14-17)
Verses 1-7 Believers are beautiful, as clothed in the righteousness of Christ; and fragrant, as adorned with the graces of his Spirit; and they thrive under the refreshing beams of the Sun of righteousness. The lily is a very noble plant in the East; it grows to a considerable height, but has a weak stem. The church is weak in herself, yet is strong in Him that supports her. The wicked, the daughters of this world, who have no love to Christ, are as thorns, worthless and useless, noxious and hurtful. Corruptions are thorns in the flesh; but the lily now among thorns, shall be transplanted into that paradise where there is no brier or thorn. The world is a barren tree to the soul; but Christ is a fruitful one. And when poor souls are parched with convictions of sin, with the terrors of the law, or the troubles of this world, weary and heavy laden, they may find rest in Christ. It is not enough to pass by this shadow, but we must sit down under it. Believers have tasted that the Lord Jesus is gracious; his fruits are all the precious privileges of the new covenant, purchased by his blood, and communicated by his Spirit; promises are sweet to a believer, and precepts also. Pardons are sweet, and peace of conscience sweet. If our mouths are out of taste for the pleasures of sin, Divine consolations will be sweet to us. Christ brings the soul to seek and to find comforts through his ordinances, which are as a banqueting-house where his saints feast with him. The love of Christ, manifested by his death, and by his word, is the banner he displays, and believers resort to it. How much better is it with the soul when sick from love to Christ, than when surfeited with the love of this world! And though Christ seemed to have withdrawn, yet he was even then a very present help. All his saints are in his hand, which tenderly holds their aching heads. Finding Christ thus nigh to her, the soul is in great care that her communion with him is not interrupted. We easily grieve the Spirit by wrong tempers. Let those who have comfort, fear sinning it away.
[Song.2.8-Song.2.13]
Verses 8-13 The church pleases herself with thoughts of further communion with Christ. None besides can speak to the heart. She sees him come. This may be applied to the prospect the Old Testament saints had of Christ's coming in the flesh. He comes as pleased with his own undertaking. He comes speedily. Even when Christ seems to forsake, it is but for a moment; he will soon return with everlasting loving-kindness. The saints of old saw him, appearing through the sacrifices and ceremonial institutions. We see him through a glass darkly, as he manifests himself through the lattices. Christ invites the new convert to arise from sloth and despondency, and to leave sin and worldly vanities, for union and communion with him. The winter may mean years passed in ignorance and sin, unfruitful and miserable, or storms and tempests that accompanied his conviction of guilt and danger. Even the unripe fruits of holiness are pleasant unto Him whose grace has produced them. All these encouraging tokens and evidences of Divine favour, are motives to the soul to follow Christ more fully. Arise then, and come away from the world and the flesh, come into fellowship with Christ. This blessed change is owing wholly to the approaches and influences of the Sun of righteousness.
[Song.2.14-Song.2.17]
Verses 14-17 The church is Christ's dove; she returns to him, as her Noah. Christ is the Rock, in whom alone she can think herself safe, and find herself easy, as a dove in the hole of a rock, when struck at by the birds of prey. Christ calls her to come boldly to the throne of grace, having a great High Priest there, to tell what her request is. Speak freely, fear not a slight or a repulse. The voice of prayer is sweet and acceptable to God; those who are sanctified have the best comeliness. The first risings of sinful thoughts and desires, the beginnings of trifling pursuits which waste the time, trifling visits, small departures from truth, whatever would admit some conformity to the world; all these, and many more, are little foxes which must be removed. This is a charge to believers to mortify their sinful appetites and passions, which are as little foxes, that destroy their graces and comforts, and crush good beginnings. Whatever we find a hinderance to us in that which is good, we must put away. He feedeth among the lilies; this shows Christ's gracious presence among believers. He is kind to all his people. It becomes them to believe this, when under desertion and absence, and so to ward off temptations. The shadows of the Jewish dispensation were dispelled by the dawning of the gospel day. And a day of comfort will come after a night of desertion. Come over the mountains of Bether, "the mountains that divide," looking forward to that day of light and love. Christ will come over every separating mountain to take us home to himself.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe trials of the church by the withdrawing of Christ.1–5The excellences of the church, The care of Christ for her.6–11
Seeking Christ when his presence seems withdrawn (verses 1–5)

For the Old Testament church, discerning Christ through the ceremonial law was difficult. Its watchmen often gave little assistance to those seeking him.

Night can picture spiritual coldness, darkness, drowsiness and uncertainty.

When believers first become troubled by a loss of felt fellowship with Christ, they may make only weak attempts to recover that comfort. When these efforts fail, they are stirred to greater diligence.

The streets and squares suggest the appointed means of grace in which we should seek the Lord. The soul asks those responsible for watching over others, but still does not immediately find satisfaction.

We must not stop at the outward means. By faith, turn directly to Christ.

Taking hold of him and refusing to let go pictures persistent, humble prayer joined with active faith in his promises.

The Lord is not offended by earnest requests from believers who cling to him in faith. He welcomes such pleading.

A person who has found the Savior wants to help others know him too.

Wherever Christ is found, welcome him into our homes and especially our hearts.

Let us remind ourselves and one another not to grieve the Holy Spirit, our Comforter, or provoke the withdrawal of the Beloved's comforting presence.

Christ safely carries his people through the wilderness (verses 6–11)

The wilderness pictures the present world. Believers come out of it when they turn away from its sinful pleasures, goals and patterns and seek happiness in fellowship with the Savior.

Through the Comforter's guidance, even a poor and weary soul will rise like incense from the altar, with affections directed toward heaven.

The Holy Spirit makes the believer's devotion lively and fills the heart with heavenly graces.

Christ is the Peace of his people and the King of heavenly Zion. He has prepared a safe way to carry his redeemed through the wilderness.

The decorated bed or portable litter represents a place of rest and secure travel, made splendid in a manner befitting its owner.

The church is strongly guarded: more are with her than against her. Even when believers fear the dangers of night, they are safe when resting in Christ.

Henry understands the chariot as a picture of the covenant of redemption and the way of salvation, designed both for Christ's glory and for the comfort of his people, securely ordered in every part.

The purple covering represents the blood of the covenant, which shelters believers from divine wrath and the storms of this life.

At its center is Christ's love surpassing knowledge, on which believers rest.

The crown points to the honor, power and kingship belonging to Christ as he reveals himself through the gospel.

[Song.3.1-Song.3.5]
Chapter 3
The trials of the church by the withdrawing of Christ. (Song 3:1-5) The excellences of the church, The care of Christ for her. (Song 3:6-11)
Verses 1-5 It was hard to the Old Testament church to find Christ in the ceremonial law; the watchmen of that church gave little assistance to those who sought after him. The night is a time of coldness, darkness, and drowsiness, and of dim apprehensions concerning spiritual things. At first, when uneasy, some feeble efforts are made to obtain the comfort of communion with Christ. This proves in vain; the believer is then roused to increased diligence. The streets and broad-ways seem to imply the means of grace in which the Lord is to be sought. Application is made to those who watch for men's souls. Immediate satisfaction is not found. We must not rest in any means, but by faith apply directly to Christ. The holding of Christ, and not letting him go, denotes earnest cleaving to him. What prevails is a humble, ardent suing by prayer, with a lively exercise of faith on his promises. So long as the faith of believers keeps hold of Christ, he will not be offended at their earnest asking, yea, he is well pleased with it. The believer desires to make others acquainted with his Saviour. Wherever we find Christ, we must take him home with us to our houses, especially to our hearts; and we should call upon ourselves and each other, to beware of grieving our holy Comforter, and provoking the departure of the Beloved.
[Song.3.6-Song.3.11]
Verses 6-11 A wilderness is an emblem of the world; the believer comes out of it when he is delivered from the love of its sinful pleasures and pursuits, and refuses to comply with its customs and fashions, to seek happiness in communion with the Saviour. A poor soul shall come up, at last, under the conduct of the Comforter; like a cloud of incense ascending from the altar, or the smoke of the burnt-offerings. This signifies pious and devout affections, and the mounting of the soul heaven-ward. The believer is filled with the graces of God's Spirit; his devotions now are very lively. These graces and comforts are from the heavenly Canaan. He, who is the Peace of his people, the King of the heavenly Zion, has provided for the safe conveyance of his redeemed through the wilderness of this world. The bed, or palanquin, was contrived for rest and easy conveyance, but its beauty and magnificence showed the quality of its owner. The church is well guarded; more are with her than are against her: believers, when they repose in Christ, and with him, though they have their fears in the night, are yet safe. The chariot here denotes the covenant of redemption, the way of our salvation. This is that work of Christ, which makes him loved and admired in the eyes of believers. It is framed and contrived, both for the glory of Christ, and for the comfort of believers; it is well ordered in all things and sure. The blood of the covenant, that rich purple, is the cover of this chariot, by which believers are sheltered from the wind and storms of Divine wrath, and the troubles of this world; but the midst of it is that love of Christ which passes knowledge, this is for believers to repose upon. Christ, in his gospel, manifests himself. Take special notice of his crown. Applying this to Christ, it speaks the honour put upon him, and his power and dominion.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesChrist sets forth the graces of the church.1–7Christ's love to the church.8–15The church desires further influences of Divine grace.16
Christ praises the graces of his church (verses 1–7)

Henry cautions readers against giving a confident spiritual meaning to every detail of every comparison in this poem. Many such explanations are uncertain, and fanciful guesses can lead to serious mistakes.

The mountain of myrrh appears to him to refer to Mount Moriah, where the temple stood, incense was offered and God's people worshiped.

Christ was present there until the shadows of Moses' law gave way to the dawn of the gospel and the rising of the Sun of Righteousness.

Though Christ, in his human nature, is absent from his earthly church until the heavenly day breaks, he remains spiritually present with his people through his appointed ordinances.

How beautiful believers become when they are justified through Christ's righteousness and adorned with spiritual graces!

Their thoughts, words and actions remain imperfect but are increasingly pure, showing hearts nourished by the gospel.

Christ's love and protection (verses 8–15)

Christ's call to his church has two aspects.

First, it is a command to turn away from the world. Its mountains may appear pleasant, but they conceal lions and leopards—dangers for the soul.

Second, it is a promise: people will be gathered into the church from many places, and the Lord will finally deliver his people from persecution. For now they may dwell among lions (Psalm 57:4).

Christ's heart is with his church, where he has placed his treasure. He delights in its love toward him, shown both in the heart and in action.

The bride's perfume pictures the gifts and graces of the Spirit. Love and obedience please Christ more than sacrifices or incense.

Christ has clothed his people with his righteousness and given them holy joy and consolation. He walks in his garden, though unseen.

He has placed a protective hedge around it that the powers of darkness cannot break.

Believers' souls are like enclosed gardens containing a well of living water, the work of the Holy Spirit (John 4:14; 7:38).

The world does not know this saving fountain, and its enemies cannot corrupt it.

The fruits and spices picture believers and the graces growing within them. They are planted, not self-generated; precious and lasting beyond the fading flowers of this life.

When grace reaches glory, it will endure forever.

Christ is the source that makes every garden fruitful.

The church asks for the Spirit's renewing work (verse 16)

The church prays for the Holy Spirit to make the garden of the soul fruitful.

Its spices represent the precious graces worked within believers. The Spirit acts like wind: a north wind bringing conviction and a south wind bringing comfort.

He awakens holy desires and produces both the willing and the doing of what is good.

The church invites Christ to enjoy the garden. Everything growing there already belongs to him.

Let him receive the honor of its fruit; may we enjoy the comfort of knowing that he accepts it.

A believer cannot rightly rejoice in spiritual fruit unless it contributes to Christ's glory.

This was his residence till the shadows of the law given to Moses were dispersed by the breaking of the gospel day, and the rising of the Sun of righteousness. And though, in respect of his human nature, Christ is absent from his church on earth, and will continue to be so till the heavenly day break, yet he is spiritually present in his ordinances, and with his people. How fair and comely are believers, when justified in Christ's righteousness, and adorned with spiritual graces! when their thoughts, words, and deeds, though imperfect, are pure, manifesting a heart nourished by the gospel!

The church shall be delivered from her persecutors in due time, though now she dwells among lions, Ps. 57:4. Christ's heart is upon his church; his treasure is therein; and he delights in the affection she has for him; its working in the heart, and its works in the life. Christ having put upon his spouse the white raiment of his own righteousness, and the righteousness of saints, and perfumed it with holy joy and comfort, he is well pleased with it. And Christ walks in his garden unseen. A hedge of protection is made around, which all the powers of darkness cannot break through. The souls of believers are as gardens enclosed, where is a well of living water, John 4:14; 7:38, the influences of the Holy Spirit. The world knows not these wells of salvation, nor can any opposer corrupt this fountain. Saints in the church, and graces in the saints, are fitly compared to fruits and spices. They are planted, and do not grow of themselves. They are precious; they are the blessings of this earth. They will be kept to good purpose when flowers are withered. He stirs up good affections, and works in us both to will and to do that which is good. The church invites Christ. Christ welcomes his people's invitation (verse 1)

See how readily Christ accepts his people's invitation!

Whatever small measure of goodness remains in us would disappear unless he preserved it.

He also invites those he loves to eat and drink abundantly: the acts of worship in which his people honor him are means through which he gives grace.

Carelessness interrupts fellowship with Christ (verses 2–8)

Churches and individual believers may, through carelessness and false security, provoke Christ to withdraw the comfort of his presence.

We should recognize our periods of spiritual slumber and unhealthy attitudes.

Christ knocks to awaken us through his word and Spirit, through difficulties and through conscience. Henry points to Revelation 3:20.

Even when we neglect Christ, he does not forget us. His love should move us to respond with love, including acts of self-denial; such surrender benefits us.

Careless souls make little of the Lord Jesus. We cannot send someone else to open the door for us.

We make excuses: we have no desire, no strength or no time. But these excuses amount to taking Christ lightly. Refusing to leave a warm bed or face a cold wind for him is a kind of contempt.

The image of the Bridegroom putting his hand to the door represents the powerful influence of God's grace and the Spirit working upon the heart.

The sweet-smelling myrrh on the door handles represents the believer rising above self-indulgence, seeking Christ in prayer and removing obstacles to fellowship.

Yet the Beloved has gone away. Through this loss of felt communion, Christ teaches believers to prize his gracious visits more highly.

Nevertheless, the soul still calls him her Beloved. The sense of desertion does not necessarily mean despair.

We may confess both faith and weakness: “Lord, I believe; help my unbelief.”

Once God awakens us, memories of ignored conviction and rejected invitations become painfully bitter.

The believer searches diligently, not only praying but also seeking Christ in the places and ways where he is ordinarily found.

The watchmen wound her. Henry notes that some interpreters understand this as ministers applying God's word wrongly to people with awakened consciences.

Her appeal to the daughters of Jerusalem expresses the distressed believer's desire even for the prayers of the weakest Christian.

An awakened soul feels Christ's withdrawal more keenly than any outward distress.

The church praises Christ's excellence (verses 9–16)

Even people who know little of Christ may notice something beautiful in believers who bear his likeness.

When people begin to ask about his character and perfections, there is reason for hope.

Christians who know him should eagerly help others know him too.

To a heart enlightened to discern spiritual things, his divine glory makes him altogether lovely.

Henry interprets his white appearance as the innocence of Christ's spotless life, and his red appearance as the blood shed in his suffering and death.

The other images belong to the figurative language of their original time, depicting bodily beauty and gracious character. We may not immediately understand every allusion.

Christ will ultimately be glorified in his saints and admired by everyone who believes.

May his love constrain us to live for his glory.

Those who hear of Christ seek him (verse 1)

People who learn something of Christ's excellence and of the comfort of belonging to him naturally want to know where they may find him.

Anyone wishing to find Christ must seek him early and diligently.

Christ among his people (verses 2 and 3)

Christ's church is like a sheltered garden, set apart from the world. He cares for it, visits it and delights in it.

Those wishing to find him should attend the means through which he makes himself known: his word, the sacraments and prayer.

When Christ comes among his people, he comes to welcome his friends and also to take believers to himself.

Henry pictures him gathering his lilies one by one. At the final day he will send angels to gather them all, so that he may be glorified in them.

The death of a believer is like a gardener picking a treasured flower. Christ preserves that flower from fading and causes it to flourish forever, with increasing beauty.

If our conscience can testify that we truly belong to Christ, we need not doubt his commitment to us: the covenant will not fail on his side.

The church takes comfort in knowing that Christ finds delight among the lilies—his own redeemed people.

Christ's praise of the church (verses 4–10)

Every genuine form of holiness on earth belongs to the life of Christ's church.

Christ continues conquering his enemies, while believers fight and gain victories over the world, sinful desires and the devil.

He shows tenderness toward the people he redeemed and delights in the work of his own grace within them.

Only true believers possess the beauty of holiness, and when their real character becomes evident, that beauty will be recognized.

At conversion, believers resemble the morning dawn: their light is still small but growing.

In sanctification, the church is fair as the moon, receiving every ray of holiness and grace from Christ.

In justification, believers are clear as the sun, clothed in the righteousness of Christ, the Sun of Righteousness.

Under his banner they persevere in the spiritual fight of faith.

The Spirit's work and the Shulammite (verses 11–13)

Christian character grows through private reflection and meditation, but not through lazy, self-indulgent withdrawal from responsibility.

When ordinary duties allow some quiet, the believer no longer finds the world's entertainments attractive.

Instead, the heart prays that the things belonging to God's Spirit may grow within it and around it.

The world may misunderstand this life and imagine such a person has abandoned true interests. In fact the believer is occupied with matters of lasting worth.

A humble Christian may prefer to avoid public notice, yet the Lord delights to honor that person.

Henry also sees a possible reference here to angels sent to receive a believer's soul at death. Their arrival may startle the departing Christian, but the Lord will be that soul's strength and eternal portion.

Henry understands the title Shulammite to signify perfection and peace. The church does not possess these in herself but in Christ—complete through his righteousness, reconciled by his blood and given peace by his Spirit.

The beauty of holiness in the church (verses 1–9)

The images in this chapter differ from those used earlier. Henry explains that their original language evokes splendid and beautiful clothing.

The saints have such honor through being clothed with Christ. Their character should make the teaching of God their Savior attractive in every respect.

Believers who act consistently with their confession honor Christ, commend the gospel and may awaken sinners to its truth.

The church is compared to a tall, spreading palm tree. Her love for Christ and the obedience arising from that love bear precious fruit from the true Vine.

The King is pictured among the galleries. Christ delights in the assemblies and appointed worship of his people. He takes pleasure in the fruit of his own grace within them.

These images describe the beauty of holiness in the church and in each believer, who will ultimately be presented to the heavenly Bridegroom.

The church desires deeper fellowship with Christ (verses 10–13)

The church rejoices that she belongs to Christ and that Christ belongs to her.

She humbly asks him to walk with her, guiding, teaching and comforting her. She wants to speak freely with him about every need and grief, without interruption.

All who have been made holy sincerely desire this fellowship. Those who would walk with Christ must turn away from the world's sinful attractions.

We can enjoy communion with God wherever he places us. We should never go willingly somewhere we cannot ask him in faith to accompany us.

Begin seeking him early: early in life and early each day. Even a poor dwelling becomes pleasant through God's presence, while the loveliest countryside cannot satisfy a soul that lacks the Beloved.

Our souls are vineyards. They should produce useful fruit, and we should frequently ask whether our lives are bearing righteousness.

Christ's presence makes the vines flourish, as sunlight renews a garden. If we can sincerely say to him, “You know all things; you know that I love you,” and if his Spirit assures us that our souls are growing, we have reason for confidence.

Yet we must also ask him to search our hearts and show us our true condition.

Every gracious act and fruit of holiness pleases Jesus. Keep such fruits ready for him, so that by bearing much fruit we glorify him.

All grace comes from Christ; therefore all its fruit should be offered to Christ.

Such honour have all his saints; and having put on Christ, they are distinguished by their beautiful and glorious apparel. They adorn the doctrine of God their Saviour in all things. Consistent believers honour Christ, recommend the gospel, and convince and awaken sinners. The church resembles the stately and spreading palm; while her love for Christ, and the obedience resulting therefrom, are precious fruit of the true Vine. The King is held in the galleries. Christ takes delight in the assemblies and ordinances of his people; and admires the fruit of his grace in them. When applied to the church and to each faithful Christian, all this denotes that beauty of holiness, in which they shall be presented to their heavenly Bridegroom.

Verses 10-13 The church, the believing soul, triumphs in its relation to Christ, and interest in him. She humbly desires communion with him. Let us walk together, that I may receive counsel, instruction, and comfort from thee; and may make known my wants and my grievances to thee, with freedom, and without interruption. Communion with Christ is what all that are made holy earnestly breathe after. And those who would converse with Christ, must go forth from the world. Wherever we are, we may keep up communion with God. Nor should we go where we cannot in faith ask him to go with us. Those who would go abroad with Christ, must begin early in the morning of their days; must begin every day with him, seek him early, seek him diligently. A gracious soul can reconcile itself to the poorest places, if it may have communion with God in them; but the most delightful fields will not satisfy, unless the Beloved is there. Let us not think to be satisfied with any earthly object. Our own souls are our vineyards; they should be planted with useful trees. We should often search whether we are fruitful in righteousness. Christ's presence will make the vine flourish, and the tender grapes appear, as the returning sun revives the gardens. If we can appeal to him, Thou knowest all things, thou knowest that I love thee; if his Spirit witness with our spirit, that our souls prosper, it is enough. And we must beg of him to search and try us, to discover us to ourselves. The fruits and exercises of graces are pleasant to the Lord Jesus. These must be laid up, and always ready; that by our bringing forth much fruit, he may be glorified. It is all from him, therefore it is fit it should be all for him.

Longing for closer fellowship with Christ (verses 1–4)

The church longs for the open affection and constant closeness that brothers and sisters share. By grace believers become participants in God's nature, and Christ has become their Brother.

Wherever we meet him, let us acknowledge our relationship to him and our love for him without fearing the contempt of others.

Do we truly desire to serve Christ more faithfully? What fruits of holiness have we prepared to express our love for him?

The church warns her children not to drive away Christ's gracious presence. When tempted, we should remind ourselves not to grieve the Holy Spirit.

Love that survives every trial (verses 5–7)

The Jewish church came out of the wilderness through God's power and favor. Christ's grace also raised his church from a desolate condition.

A sinful life is a wilderness without true comfort. We cannot escape by relying on our own reasoning or righteousness. We must lean upon Christ, the Lord our Righteousness, by faith.

The church asks to remain secure in Christ's heart and under his protection, like a seal impressed upon his heart.

Those who love him fear anything that would draw them away—especially their own actions, which might interrupt the comfort of fellowship.

No flood can drown Christ's love for his people. Neither threats nor attractions of the world should lessen our love for him. His love strengthens believers against both persecution and prosperity's temptations.

The church prays and works for others (verses 8–12)

Henry sees the church here interceding for the Gentiles, who had not yet received God's word and the ordinary means of grace.

People brought to Christ should seek ways to bring others to him. Stronger Christians should constantly pray for those who are young or weak in faith.

The images of a wall and door suggest a church founded securely on Christ, the precious Foundation and Cornerstone, and a lasting entrance through the removed barrier between peoples.

The Lord promises his care for those not yet called, and the church should likewise remain concerned for them.

Our hearts are vineyards to be guarded diligently. All their fruit belongs to Christ's praise. Serving him is no loss: those who labor for him ultimately receive a far greater gain.

The prayer for Christ's return (verses 13 and 14)

At the close of this dialogue, Christ addresses the church dwelling in the gardens—among his people and in their appointed worship.

He calls her to persevere in prayer and praise, which delight him. She responds by asking him to return quickly and bring her fully into his presence.

Until that day, Christ is in heaven, pictured as mountains of sweet spices. At the appointed time, every eye will see him in the glory of the world to come.

Believers look forward to that day and seek to be ready for it. They should faithfully fulfill their present duties, so that others may see their good works and glorify the Father.

Continuing in prayer and thanksgiving, we may grow in joy and strength and look toward death and judgment without fear.

Even so, come, Lord Jesus.

A sinful state is a wilderness in which there is no true comfort; it is a wandering, wanting state: There is no coming out of this wilderness, but leaning on Christ as our Beloved, by faith; not leaning to our own understanding, nor trusting in any righteousness of our own; but in the strength of him, who is the Lord our Righteousness. Those who truly love Christ, are jealous of every thing that would draw them from him; especially of themselves, lest they should do any thing to provoke him to withdraw from them. If we love Christ, the fear of coming short of his love, or the temptations to forsake him, will be most painful to us. No waters can quench Christ's love to us, nor any floods drown it. Let nothing abate our love to him. Nor will life, and all its comforts, entice a believer from loving Christ. If the beginning of this work were likened to a wall built upon Him the precious Foundation and Corner-stone, then the Gentile church would become as a palace for the great King, built of solid silver. If the first preaching of the gospel were as the making a door through the wall of partition, that door should be lasting, as cased with boards of durable cedar. She shall be carefully and effectually protected, enclosed so as to receive no damage. The church is full of care for those yet uncalled. True believers as they are looking for, so they are hastening to the coming of that day of the Lord. Continuing earnest in prayer for what we want, our thanksgivings will abound, and our joy will be full; our souls will be enriched, and our labours prospered. We shall be enabled to look forward to death and judgment without fear. Even so, come, Lord Jesus.
